name: @nanorix/mcp-server

tools.name: nanorix_create_capsule
tools.description: Open a sealed, ephemeral Nanorix capsule to handle regulated or sensitive data (PHI, PII, financial, credentials). Each command in the capsule runs in its own Linux namespaces and root filesystem; the capsule's data directories are memory-backed (tmpfs) and are overwritten and unmounted when it is destroyed, and it then emits an AuditProof — cryptographic evidence of what ran and that the data was destroyed. Each command runs in its own user namespace. Where the API runs as root, which includes the hosted service and the documented Kubernetes profiles, each capsule leases its own non-root user and group ID for its life, and each command drops to them before its user namespace is made, so the host kernel's file-permission checks treat the command's processes as that unprivileged user. Capsules run only after a startup self-test sees a probe command hold the leased IDs with no supplementary groups and be refused when it opens /proc/sysrq-trigger, and again when it opens /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern, for writing. Call this FIRST: it returns a capsule_id you then pass to nanorix_upload / nanorix_exec / nanorix_download and finally nanorix_destroy. You declare data_classification and metadata; Nanorix never infers them.

capsulefile.description: ID of the Capsulefile to run (the sealed runtime + entrypoint + files the capsule boots from). Use nanorix_list_capsulefiles to discover available IDs.

data_classification.description: Customer-declared sensitivity of the data the capsule will handle. Nanorix never inspects or infers this — you declare it. Stored in the AuditProof's capsule context.

metadata.description: Optional customer-defined string key/value context bound into the AuditProof (max 16 keys, 64-char keys, 256-char values, 4 KB total). Keys beginning with 'nanorix:' are reserved and rejected.

max_lifetime_seconds.description: Optional hard ceiling on capsule lifetime before automatic reclamation.

tools.name: nanorix_exec
tools.description: Execute a command inside a running sealed capsule and return its stdout, stderr, and exit code. Use this to run the regulated workload after creating the capsule and uploading any input files. The command runs in its own Linux namespaces and its own root filesystem, which holds read-only system directories, six device nodes, a fresh /proc and the capsule's memory-backed workspace and does not mount the host's other paths or other capsules' directories, apart from a read-only directory holding the socket of the capsule's own sealed HTTP daemon when an egress profile is bound. If isolation setup fails, the command does not run. Each command runs in its own user namespace. Where the API runs as root, which includes the hosted service and the documented Kubernetes profiles, each capsule leases its own non-root user and group ID for its life, and each command drops to them before its user namespace is made, so the host kernel's file-permission checks treat the command's processes as that unprivileged user. Capsules run only after a startup self-test sees a probe command hold the leased IDs with no supplementary groups and be refused when it opens /proc/sysrq-trigger, and again when it opens /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern, for writing.

capsule_id.description: ID of a running capsule (from nanorix_create_capsule).

command.description: Command to execute inside the capsule. If omitted, the Capsulefile's entrypoint runs.

input_data.description: Optional data written to /data/input/uploads/data inside the capsule before the command runs (max 512 KB, counted as UTF-8 bytes). It is not sent to stdin.

tools.name: nanorix_upload
tools.description: Upload an input file into a running capsule's input directory before executing the workload. Provide text content directly, or base64 for binary data. Returns the file reference and its SHA-512 content hash (the hash is bound into the AuditProof).

capsule_id.description: ID of a running capsule (from nanorix_create_capsule).

filename.description: Name the file will have inside the capsule's input directory.

content.description: File contents. Plain text by default, or base64 when encoding='base64'.

encoding.description: How `content` is encoded. Use 'base64' for binary files; defaults to 'utf8'.

tools.name: nanorix_download
tools.description: Download an output file produced by a capsule's workload. Do this BEFORE destroying the capsule — once destroyed, only the AuditProof remains and the data is gone. Returns the file content (text or base64) and its SHA-512 hash for integrity checking.

capsule_id.description: ID of the capsule whose output you want to retrieve.

filename.description: Name of the output file to download from the capsule.

encoding.description: How to return `content`. Use 'base64' for binary output; defaults to 'utf8'.

tools.name: nanorix_get_auditproof
tools.description: Fetch the AuditProof JSON for a capsule. The AuditProof is the cryptographic record of the capsule's lifecycle — an 8-step SHA-512 hash chain plus an Ed25519 attestation. Retrieve it after destroying the capsule, then pass it to nanorix_verify_auditproof to confirm its integrity independently.

capsule_id.description: ID of a destroyed capsule whose AuditProof you want to fetch.

tools.name: nanorix_verify_auditproof
tools.description: Independently verify the cryptographic AuditProof an agent's capsule produced. Runs entirely offline (no API key, no network) and re-derives the 8-step SHA-512 hash chain and the Ed25519 signature. Returns PASS or FAIL plus the failing step on mismatch. This is a STRUCTURAL integrity check (the chain and signature are intact) — it is not a regulatory or compliance judgement; an auditor certifies regulatory adequacy. Unless the proof was given as a string that is not JSON, the result includes verification_scope, which says what PASS covers: the signing key is the one the proof carries and was not resolved against a trust chain. Use this whenever you or a downstream consumer need to trust what a capsule did without trusting the Nanorix API.

proof.description: The AuditProof to verify, as either a JSON object or a JSON string. Typically the value returned by nanorix_get_auditproof or nanorix_destroy.

tools.name: nanorix_destroy
tools.description: Destroy a capsule. This cryptographically shreds its volatile memory and data, then returns the terminal AuditProof — the evidence of what ran and that the data was destroyed. Always download any output you need (nanorix_download) BEFORE calling this: after destruction only the AuditProof remains. Pass the returned proof to nanorix_verify_auditproof to confirm it independently.

capsule_id.description: ID of the capsule to destroy.

tools.name: nanorix_status
tools.description: Check a capsule's current lifecycle status (e.g. active, destroyed). Use this to decide your next step — whether the capsule is still running and accepting commands/uploads, or already destroyed (in which case fetch its AuditProof with nanorix_get_auditproof).

capsule_id.description: ID of the capsule to inspect.

tools.name: nanorix_list_capsulefiles
tools.description: List the customer's available Capsulefiles (the sealed runtime + entrypoint + file definitions a capsule boots from). Call this to discover which capsulefile ID to pass to nanorix_create_capsule. Takes no arguments.
